Inget likt de tidigare två "Toy Story" filmerna som höll en hög kvalitet av lättsam humor, acceptabel moral och för filmen logisk konsekvens. Denna filmen erbjuder inget i stil med föregångarna, denna filmen behandlar istället mycket mörka koncept som inte angår barn: tortyr, hjärntvätt, fångenskap, våld, manipulation, lögn, svek, mord, sexuellt utnyttjande etc. och en kass moral om ovänskap, livstragik och oförmågan till omvändelse och förlåtelse. Leksakerna har helt tappat fokuset på välbehag och samkväm och strider istället relativt våldsamt och förfärligt i en dödskamp a la förtvivlan och mafiautpressning. Konstiga och olämpliga koncept introduceras till en ung audiens i denna avbrytande otematiska katastrof till uppföljare. Ej sevärd, det är bara en konstig och överflödig money grab av Toy Story varumärket.

This entry confirms that toys feel discomfort, pain, and can also recognize the true horror that is death of self. In the face of these realizations, they are confronted with the question of is it better to be devoted to one “owner”, one source of love, and consider life worthwhile? Or spend their unending existence, periodically bouncing between differing partners with which to provide “play” time, until their brief period of use runs its course? Much to ponder

This was really good. I liked the story a lot more than I expected and I can understand why this one is so loved. The idea of Andy growing up and having to decide what to do with his old toys gives the film a much more emotional side. Woody, Buzz and the rest of the gang are still so lovable and I enjoyed seeing them all together again. The new characters are also fun, especially Lotso, who looks adorable at first but turns out to be a surprisingly good villain. I also liked the setting in the daycare. It gives the film a completely different atmosphere and creates some really funny and exciting moments. The animation still looks beautiful and the action is surprisingly intense at times. The ending was definitely the best part for me. Even though I don't have the same childhood attachment to Toy Story as a lot of people do, I could still feel how emotional that moment was.

What made the first two Toy Story films work so well was the sense of deeper characterisation and internal conflict that formed an emotional backbone for the toys’ colourful adventures; Woody learning to accept Buzz in the first film or weighing the decision to become a museum piece in the second both served as the kind of substantial character arc that is conspicuously absent from the third, which here reduces him to a righteous Cassandra figure trying to rescue his friends from daycare well before its hidden darkness is revealed (a saviour complex that the fourth film correctly chooses to deconstruct in order to properly close the loop on him as a character). In trying to give the toys what was presumably going to be one last adventure, it sacrifices that particular sense of character for the sake of a perfunctory prison-break parody and a handful of precisely-calibrated emotional moments around which the entire film seems to have been reverse-engineered. The recent sequels had their flaws, but they still understood the need to give these toys some semblance of interiority that could be challenged by more than just the excitement and thrills posed by external obstacles - as a result, the inclusion of a Totoro doll seem less like one iconic studio tipping its cap to another than it does an ironic reminder of how far removed Pixar could get from Ghibli’s nuanced approach to animation.

A remarkably boring sequel only remembered for its last 15 minutes. Story is a stunning departure from the creativity, wit, and intelligence of the first two films, with its never-funny script, downgraded character writing, and predictable narrative. Opening sequence and many other story details are notably derivative as lame nostalgia-copies of earlier material. As with most in Pixar's 2000s output, film's animation is flat and generic. Antagonist's backstory is shallow and his outcome anticlimactic. Has many terrible plot holes & conveniences and way too many new characters. Inciting incident, general plot, and pacing are all ok. Rating: C+

11 years on from Toy Story 2, the trilogy was completed with an epic prison escape movie written to close out the franchise. Toy Story 3 is a film I’m very conflicted on, because in fleeting moments I catch the brilliance the high letterboxd score would suggest and the third act is (mostly) as good as they say. The ending is enough to make any grown man sniffle, it would have been a great place to leave the franchise if it didn’t ultimately continue. But I have serious gripes with the film I can’t ignore, that frankly leave it well short of the first two films in the Toy Story trilogy turned pentalogy Firstly a brief note on the creation process. Toy Story 3 began life in 2004, remaining at the tentative stage due to the complications of the Disney deal I touch on in my Toy Story 1 and 2 reviews. Eventually Disney bought out the company, and work was restarted on Toy Story 3 with a new script and an absurd $200 million budget. That is over twice the budget of Toy Story 2 which I remind you was scrapped and restarted entirely. In 2010 the movie finally released to much critical and commercial success, becoming the fourth highest grossing film of all time (now barely in the top 50, inflation is a funny thing) and featuring on multiple top 10 films of the 2010s lists The film mostly moves away from the A plot B plot structure of the first two films and instead has the gang almost entirely together. Woody has a short stint away from the Daycare, outside of that we stick with the entire cast of toys the whole way through. Getting some big problems out the way early, the cast here is not even half as good as they were in Toy Story 2. Mr Potato Head is a shell of his former self, Ham might as well be an extra, Slinky has been neutered to having no jokes at all, Jessie has much less bite than her debut appearance. I laughed maybe twice, three times the entire film. Meanwhile Toy Story 2 had me in stitches the whole way through. The biggest casualty is Buzz, who they so clearly have no fucking idea what to do with so they do a ‘Buzz is back to his default setting’ story AGAIN. In all three of the original Toy Story trilogy we have Buzz thinking he’s not a toy, that’s absolutely egregious. The second justifies it with it being a seperate Buzz and the comedy being on point, here he’s placed in an antagonist role and it’s ass. Speaking of ass and antagonists, Lotso fucking sucks. It’s just stinky Pete but again! It’s the exact same villain but worse in every conceivable way. One of Disney’s worst villains, a complete charisma vacuum who is half baked and poorly written The themes of Toy Story 3 are around growing up, moving on, accepting that things change and making peace with that. At least, that’s what the final act would suggest. But unlike the first two films which did a brilliant job to make the plot contribute to the greater themes being explored, Toy Story 3 forces it’s ideas into the first and last 15 minutes with absolutely nothing in-between. So for a good amount of the run time, it really is just ‘woody was right the whole time 😱’ which we’ve done already and a prison escape movie. Alas, it’s not even a very good prison escape movie with the escape sequence being undercooked and not on par with the first two films action sequences. Toy Story 1 and 2 are not only funnier but more dramatically intense, Toy Story 3 uses middling jokes as a crutch for a lack of interesting stakes because again the villain is pathetic and the personal stakes for anyone other than Woody feel minuscule Yes the last stretch is great. The imagery of the incinerator rules, although the aliens saving them with the giant claw borders on Dues Ex Machina in its absurdity and somewhat undercuts the whole melting alive thing. The scene where Andy plays with the toys with Bonnie is beautiful. Woody saying ‘so long, partner’ and realising he belongs with the other Toy’s and not at College is great. I just wish these moments felt more earned, I don’t think much of anything in the second act resonates with the resolution thematically or even tonally Toy Story 3 is a misfire in the franchise for mine. It doesn’t have anywhere close to the meticulous plotting or comedic timing of the first two films, and is for mine a step below in just about every way. This includes animation by the way, the Toys move far more cartoonish with looney toons physics which takes away a huge part of the charm of the original two films. The toys actually moved like toys, in the third instalment they don’t. It’s the attention to detail that really derails the end of the trilogy for mine, and is probably why I didn’t have a visceral reaction to a fourth or fifth or sixth that others have had. I’d even argue that while Toy Story 3 has a nice ending it doesn’t wrap up the entire franchise in this perfect bow that should never have been touched. It’s the end of Andy’s story but Woody and especially Buzz don’t get anything close to satisfying conclusions to their journeys. And yet in the Andy farewell movie we spend almost all of it away from Andy… again! Wouldn’t it have made way more sense to spend more time with Andy and actually explore that relationship beyond a sense of duty. Explore the emotional dilemma Woody faces, loyalty to his best friend or acceptance that his friend grows up in a way he won’t. And how Buzz relates to that, drawing back to the first film in which Woody reacts to potential replacement with resentment and jealousy. We can see how Woody’s character has evolved through his connection to Buzz and with age. As is, this isn’t even close to the perfect farewell film people insinuate it is

Maybe I'm too cynical for my own good but I did not like this one. I was 14 when it came out and just old enough for the sentiment of one final romp with my toys to resonate that very much doesn't exist as a nearly 30 year old. Be that as it may, I still found it in my heart to appreciate the tight little movie the first one is and the second takes the themes of toys to an absolute extreme that speaks very broadly about mortality and abandonment. This movie only ever gets close in the opening, when after two movies of hijinks to keep being alive secret, the first plan is a literal desperate call to be seen. It's a futile plan everyone knew wouldn't work but what else are you supposed to do when eternity is staring you in the face? The movie falls off a cliff when they get to the daycare. The first two movies felt they did a lot to show that how a person handled a toy was an extension of who they were. Here I find the very staunch and unexplored binary of the young children "not playing right" compared to the older children dull, especially compared to the subtle details of the household that informed Sid as a character. It reminds me of something that bugged me in the Barbie movie where it's obviously selling you on how the toy is a vehicle for your imagination but still makes very clear there's a "right" way to play with it and the "right" way is always in corporate interest. Barbie is also in this movie so maybe it's a Mattel thing. There isn't much to the daycare outside of it's prison motif. Unlike The Prospector who's self loathing was birthed of never being played with and only valued as a collector's item, Lotso and his big scary baby are jokes. What if the evil prison warden was a cuddly teddy bear and his heavy was a big scary baby? These random toys gamble in shady puke green settings to establish they are evil and take joy out of running toys through the ringer but one exposed lie and quick 10 second speech about fascism from Barbie and I guess the gang did prison abolition? I actually said in my review of the first one that I didn't want to succumb to snarky literalism but it is clear that the first two movies are about "toys" in the broadest sense where they represent trust, innocence, and youth. This movie is about "toys" as literal objects. It's an exercise in melodramatic toy existentialism and gratuitous toy violence so that you feel bad for not loving plastic enough and maybe even buy some more plastic. This isn't to say that toys aren't meaningful, just to say that in the first two movies the toys are passive agents to a child's imagination. Woody himself is not special, his position as a kids favorite toy is what's special, and it's a spot you can lose at any given moment so you need to appreciate it while you can. The movie brings this idea home with the ending decently enough if you're a fan, I'm not totally heartless and it's not bad having Andy unable to give up Woody for a moment as a way to represent him uncertain about leaving that childhood behind. I just personally wish the movie was more about that tension with Andy and not masculine buff toys calling Ken gay or Latin Lover Lightyear in pre-school Alcatraz. The only thing keeping this together and me believing that Andy has an emotional connection with some squeaky toys from a pizza restaurant crane game is the fact that I've seen the first two movies.

This film felt too formulaic for me. Every single entry in this franchise has always been. This film just kind of shows. All of the three films in a way are about a toy or in this case multiple toys being displaced from their home and they have to rescue or somehow find a way back to their home. Yes, every single one of this films has a Buzz Lightyear that doesn't know he's a toy.

And here we go again… another Dicta-Toy-ship Story 3, except this time it’s this absolute unit Lotso with his so called Caterpillar Room, which is basically just a gulag or the equivalent of being sent to a Siberian prison. Or if that’s not bad enough you just get a death sentence. Woody is now just a propaganda merchant now praising Dear Supreme Leader Andy, while Buzz is just a bot so he becomes one with the system and Jessie still has Stockholm syndrome. In the end it’s soft tyranny or straight oppression… 2/5 could of been more comedic:)
